title: GraphRAG & LLM Retrieval
blurb: Tests why flat vector RAG misses multi-hop answers, entity-centric retrieval, multi-hop traversal as ordinary graph traversal, the control query that keeps the comparison honest, community summaries built from graph facts, and graph-grounded prompts.

questions.prompt: Why does flat vector RAG often miss multi-hop answers?
options: Vector databases can't store more than one passage per entity.
Similarity finds what reads alike, not what connects.
Multi-hop questions are too long to embed.
LLMs ignore retrieved passages on multi-hop questions.
questions.explanation: No single passage states "Fenwick shares a parent with a flagged vendor". Three facts must be connected, which similarity ranking doesn't do.

questions.prompt: Why did the worked example also run a single-hop control query?
options: To show GraphRAG fails on simple questions
To tune the TF-IDF weights before the main test
To check vector RAG on a one-passage answer
To measure how fast each method ran
questions.explanation: Vector RAG's top passage answered the spending question directly. GraphRAG fits relationship-shaped questions, not all questions.

questions.prompt: Is GraphRAG's multi-hop retrieval a new kind of algorithm?
options: No. It chains one-hop lookups, like BFS.
No. It is the same as TF-IDF retrieval.
Yes. It needs a learned model to choose each hop.
Yes. It replaces traversal with vector similarity.
questions.explanation: owners_of, siblings_owned_by and vendors_of are each one hop. Chaining them answers a specific question.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong if a traversal goes too many hops?
options: It reduces the graph to a single community.
It always loops forever on any graph.
It floods the context with loosely related facts.
It misses the answer entirely, as flat vector RAG did.
questions.explanation: Too few hops misses the answer. Too many floods the context. Depth is a real design choice.

questions.prompt: Why is the community summary free of hallucination risk?
options: It is string-formatted from graph facts, no LLM.
It only lists node names, never relationships.
It uses a model trained only on the graph.
It is checked against a second LLM for consistency.
questions.explanation: Every line comes from a graph fact. An LLM may polish phrasing, but shouldn't supply the facts.

questions.prompt: When is a community summary the wrong tool?
options: When the communities were found with Louvain
When the question asks about a cluster's overall risk
When asking what specifically links X and Y
When the graph has more than two communities
questions.explanation: A summary covers a cluster coarsely. A specific connection needs a precise, auditable path.

questions.prompt: Why does the graph-grounded prompt state the hop chain as explicit facts?
options: Each hop is stated, so it can be checked.
LLMs can't read raw source passages at all.
It hides the source data from the LLM.
It makes the prompt shorter than any passage.
questions.explanation: The traversal already answered the connecting question. Stating it makes the reasoning auditable.

questions.prompt: What did the TF-IDF baseline's top 3 passages miss?
options: Any mention of a holding company
Any mention of Fenwick Supplies
Any passage at all, since all scored zero
Any mention of a flagged vendor
questions.explanation: It retrieved passages sharing words like "parent" and "flagged", but the passage naming Fenwick ranked lower.

questions.prompt: How should a production system choose between vector RAG and GraphRAG, per the chapter?
options: Run both and route each query by its shape.
Use GraphRAG only when no graph exists.
Always use vector RAG, since it's simpler.
Always use GraphRAG, since it found the answer here.
questions.explanation: GraphRAG layers alongside vector RAG. Relationship-shaped questions go to the graph, single-fact lookups to vectors.

questions.prompt: What does GraphRAG need in place before it can work, per the trade-offs?
options: Nothing beyond what vector RAG already needs
A labelled set of multi-hop questions for training
A knowledge graph and the question's entities
A larger embedding model than vector RAG uses
questions.explanation: The graph comes from Chapter 78's extraction work, and anchoring needs the right entities. That setup is the cost.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in one or two sentences, why vector similarity has no way to represent "shares a parent company with," using the distinction between "what reads alike" and "what's connected."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Vector similarity measures how alike two pieces of text read semantically, based on co-occurrence patterns learned during embedding training. It has no mechanism for representing a specific, factual, structural relationship like "shares a parent company with" unless that exact relationship happens to be spelled out in text near both entities. A graph edge encodes that connection explicitly and deterministically, independent of whether any passage ever states it in similar-reading language.

bookExercises.prompt: List the three one-hop lookups Listing 80.2 chains together, and state which `networkx` API call each one uses.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The three one-hop lookups: (1) finding an entity's direct neighbors/relationships, using `G.neighbors(node)` or `G.edges(node, data=True)`; (2) filtering those neighbors by relationship type (e.g. only `OWNS` or `PURCHASES_FROM` edges), using edge attribute filtering on the same call; (3) following the resulting neighbor set one hop further, repeating the same `G.neighbors()`/`G.edges()` pattern on the new node set.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 80.1 and Listing 80.2 as a pattern, write the additional one-hop function needed to check whether two companies share the *same* parent company two levels up (i.e., a grandparent), rather than a direct parent.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A grandparent-check function would chain two one-hop parent lookups: first find company A's direct parent (one hop via `OWNS`/`PARENT_OF`-type edges), then find that parent's own parent (a second one-hop lookup from the first result), and compare the result to company B's own one-hop parent lookup. Two companies share a grandparent if both single-hop-then-single-hop chains terminate at the same node.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's control query worked because the answer sits in one passage. Using the corpus described in the Worked Example, write a second control query whose answer also sits in exactly one passage, and state which passage index answers it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Answer depends on the specific corpus described in the Worked Example. The exercise requires identifying a fact stated entirely within one passage (not requiring multi-hop combination) and citing that passage's index, analogous to how the chapter's original control query was answerable from a single passage without traversal.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 80.3, trace by hand which community `Globex Materials` would land in, given it has a `PURCHASES_FROM` edge to nothing in the Meridian Holdings cluster and no `OWNS` edges at all.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Tracing by hand: `Globex Materials` has a `PURCHASES_FROM` edge to nothing in the Meridian Holdings cluster and no `OWNS` edges at all. Since Louvain community detection groups nodes by density of interconnection, and `Globex Materials` has no edges connecting it into the Meridian Holdings cluster specifically, it would not land in the same community as Meridian Holdings; it would instead land in whichever community its actual edges (if any exist elsewhere in the graph) connect it most densely to, or form/join a separate, more sparsely-connected community.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer wants to replace their entire vector-RAG pipeline with GraphRAG because "graphs are more accurate." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say back, including what you'd ask about their actual question types first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Whether GraphRAG is more accurate depends entirely on your question types. For questions answerable from a single relevant passage, flat vector retrieval works fine and graph traversal adds unnecessary complexity; GraphRAG's real advantage is specifically on multi-hop questions where the answer requires combining facts from multiple connected passages, which vector similarity structurally cannot do. I'd want to know what fraction of your actual customer questions are genuinely multi-hop before recommending a full replacement rather than a hybrid approach."

bookExercises.prompt: A production knowledge graph has an anchor entity with very high fan-out (thousands of edges). Using the "Trade-offs" discussion of hop depth, explain what specifically goes wrong if the hop budget is left unbounded on this entity.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With unbounded hop depth on a high-fan-out anchor entity, each additional hop multiplies the candidate node set by that entity's large fan-out, causing combinatorial explosion in the number of nodes/edges considered. This both blows up compute/latency and floods the eventual context with mostly irrelevant, loosely-connected entities, diluting the genuinely relevant multi-hop connections in noise rather than surfacing them.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Edge et al. GraphRAG paper cited above. Identify one way its community-summarisation approach differs from this chapter's string-formatted summary (Listing 80.3), and explain what problem that difference solves at production scale.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The Edge et al. GraphRAG paper's community-summarisation approach typically uses an LLM to generate rich natural-language summaries of each detected community (capturing themes and relationships within it), rather than this chapter's simpler string-formatted listing of nodes/edges. The LLM-generated summary approach solves the problem of surfacing community-level insights in a form directly usable as retrieval context at production scale, where raw string-formatted community dumps would be too verbose and unstructured for an LLM to efficiently reason over.
